title: Footwear inventory planning: size runs, widths, and depth
summary: Footwear inventory planning sets depth by size and width for carryover and seasonal models. US shoe stores sell 2.1 times more in December than in January.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 23 November 2026.


Footwear inventory planning is the process of deciding how many pairs to buy and hold for each model, color, size, and width, in each store and channel, and how to keep those quantities right through reorders and transfers. Most of the difficulty comes from the size run, because one model can create more than 1,000 stock positions across a chain.


A shoe that is not available in the customer's size is, for that customer, not in the range at all. Buyers and planners at footwear retailers know this, yet most footwear inventory planning is still done and reviewed at model level, where the missing sizes are invisible.


This guide works through footwear inventory planning with one retailer followed from start to finish: what a size run costs, how to treat widths, why carryover and seasonal models need separate rules, and how to set depth per store. If you would rather test the method on your own models, you can[walk through your size and store data with our team](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


**Key Takeaways**


- One men's model in 12 sizes, two widths, and three colors has 72 variants. Across 24 stores that is 1,728 stock positions for a single model.
- In the worked example, a store that receives 36 pairs as three flat cases sells 27.4 of them and loses 8.6 pairs of demand in the core sizes, although the forecast for the model was exactly right.
- A working paper by Akchen and Caro, built on data from a footwear chain, estimates that roughly 25% of customers buy an adjacent size when theirs is missing, and its simulation holds 15% to 35% less inventory when the plan accounts for it.
- US Census Bureau data puts 2025 shoe store sales at about $34.4 billion, with December 2.1 times January and August 1.6 times September.
- The NRF expected 19.3% of online sales to be returned in 2025, which distorts demand by size if returns are not netted out.


## What is footwear inventory planning?


Footwear inventory planning is the retail process that converts a sales and margin target into pairs by model, color, size, and width for every store and channel. It covers the opening buy, the stock held in the warehouse, the replenishment rules for models that run all year, and the transfers and markdowns that close a season.


It sits under the budget, which is set by[open-to-buy planning](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/open-to-buy-planning) , and above the daily work of allocation. The budget says how much money a category may hold each month. Footwear inventory planning decides which pairs that money becomes.


Shoes share a lot with clothing, and our guide to[apparel inventory planning](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/apparel-inventory-planning) covers size curves and pre-season buys for garments. Three features set shoes apart and make footwear inventory planning a discipline of its own.


Feature Clothing Footwear


Sizes per product Often 5 to 7 Often 9 to 13, with half sizes


Second fit dimension Rare (length, petite, tall) Width, on part of the range


Fit tolerance A size up or down is often wearable Half a size can decide the sale


Display The stock is on the rail One shoe on the wall, the rest in the stockroom


## Size runs: where footwear inventory planning gets heavy


A size run is the list of sizes in which a model is bought. The run multiplies every decision in footwear inventory planning, and the multiplication is easy to underestimate when the range plan lists models and colors only.


Take a city footwear chain with 24 stores (an illustrative example with our own arithmetic, reused in every section). One of its men's leather sneakers comes in US sizes 7 to 12 with half sizes, plus size 13. That makes 12 sizes.


The model exists in two widths and three colors, so it has 72 variants. Across 24 stores, the chain manages 1,728 stock positions for that one model. A range of 150 models built the same way would produce about 260,000 positions, most of which sell less than one pair a month.


### What a flat size pack costs


Demand is not spread evenly across the run, and footwear inventory planning starts from that curve. In this example the five sizes from 9 to 11 account for 65% of sales, and the smallest and largest sizes for 2% and 3%.


Many suppliers ship in cases with a fixed mix of sizes. The simplest is a flat case of 12 pairs with one pair per size. Ingrid, who buys men's shoes for the chain, checked what a flat pack does to a store with a forecast of 36 pairs for the season (an illustrative case).


Size Demand share Pairs demanded Flat pack stock Pairs sold Lost or left


7 2% 0.7 3 0.7 2.3 left


7.5 3% 1.1 3 1.1 1.9 left


8 6% 2.2 3 2.2 0.8 left


8.5 9% 3.2 3 3.0 0.2 lost


9 12% 4.3 3 3.0 1.3 lost


9.5 14% 5.0 3 3.0 2.0 lost


10 15% 5.4 3 3.0 2.4 lost


10.5 13% 4.7 3 3.0 1.7 lost


11 11% 4.0 3 3.0 1.0 lost


11.5 6% 2.2 3 2.2 0.8 left


12 6% 2.2 3 2.2 0.8 left


13 3% 1.1 3 1.1 1.9 left


The store sells 27.4 of its 36 pairs. It loses 8.6 pairs of demand in the sizes from 8.5 to 11 and ends the season with 8.6 pairs in sizes few customers asked for. The forecast for the model was exactly right, and a quarter of the demand still went unserved.


Ingrid moved the model to a curved pack: one flat case to put every size on the shelf, then 24 pairs ordered to follow the curve. The store's stock in size 10 went from three pairs to five, and size 7 went from three pairs to one. In footwear inventory planning, the pack mix often matters more than the total quantity.


### Widths are a stock decision


In footwear inventory planning, a second width doubles the number of variants while adding little demand. If wide fittings represent 20% of sales for this model, the store sells about seven wide pairs in a season, spread over 12 sizes. That is about one pair in size 10 and close to nothing in size 7.


A wide run in every store would therefore sit almost untouched. Across the 24 stores, though, the same model sells about 170 wide pairs a season, which is enough to stock a full wide run in six stores and to serve the others from the warehouse or the web store. Footwear inventory planning has to make that choice for each model that carries a width.


Width also deserves care because fit is far from exact. A 2018 review of 18 studies by Andrew Buldt and Hylton Menz, published in the Journal of Foot and Ankle Research, reported that between 63% and 72% of participants were wearing shoes that did not accommodate the width or the length of their feet. Several of those studies covered older people or patients, so the figure is not a market average, but it shows how loosely the size sold matches the foot.


### Customers accept a neighboring size more often than plans assume


A working paper by Yi-Chun Akchen (University College London) and Felipe Caro (UCLA Anderson) looked at this with data from a large footwear chain: 51 styles of women's casual booties, nine sizes, 33 weeks of sales. As summarized by UCLA Anderson Review in May 2025, the authors estimate that roughly 25% of customers still buy the same style in an adjacent size when their own is missing.


In their simulation over a 12-week season, a plan that accounts for this holds 15% to 35% less inventory than methods that treat each size as separate. The gain is largest where stock is thin, which is the case in small stores.


For footwear inventory planning, the finding cuts two ways. A small store can live with a slightly incomplete run in the edge sizes. Substitution only helps when the neighboring size is still on the shelf, though, and in the flat pack example every core size sold out together.


## Carryover and seasonal models need separate rules


Footwear inventory planning deals with two kinds of product that behave differently. Carryover models (also called core or continuity models) stay in the range for several seasons with the same last and colors. Seasonal models are bought for one season and have no direct history.


Carryover models Seasonal models


Sales history Several seasons, by size and store None, borrowed from similar models


How stock is bought Regular replenishment orders One main buy, sometimes one reorder


Depth in store Minimum per size, refilled weekly Opening depth sized for the first weeks


Main risk Broken core sizes Leftover pairs at season end


End of life Planned run-out over months Markdown or consolidation


Mixing the two in one plan produces a known pattern in footwear inventory planning. Seasonal buys eat the budget early, and the carryover models that sell every week run short of core sizes because no money is left to refill them.


### Carryover models: replenish by size


A carryover model is replenished from the warehouse by size, each size with its own minimum. Suppose a store sells six pairs a week of a white leather sneaker. Size 10 sells about 0.9 pairs a week and size 13 about 0.18, or one pair every five to six weeks.


With weekly deliveries, the store might hold three pairs of size 10 and one pair of size 13. Now look at the chain. The 24 stores hold 72 pairs of size 10 against sales of 21.6 a week, which is 3.3 weeks of cover. They hold 24 pairs of size 13 against 4.3 a week, which is 5.6 weeks.


The edge size carries far more cover simply because one pair is the smallest amount a store can hold. This is why slow stock in carryover footwear concentrates in the smallest and largest sizes. The trigger for each refill is a reorder point by size, and our guide to the[reorder point formula](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/reorder-point-formula) covers the calculation.


One mistake we repeatedly see in footwear inventory planning is a single minimum applied to every size of a model, which starves size 10 and overstocks size 13 in the same store.


### Seasonal models: buy for a short window


Seasonal demand in footwear is steep. The US Census Bureau's Monthly Retail Trade data shows shoe store sales of about $34.4 billion in 2025. December reached $4.08 billion against $1.90 billion in January, a ratio of 2.1, and August (back to school) reached $3.86 billion against $2.41 billion in September. August and December together made up 23% of the year.


For seasonal models, footwear inventory planning works against a deadline. The model has to be in store before its window opens, and a reorder only helps if it lands in time. Tomas plans women's boots for the chain (an illustrative case). The season runs 16 weeks, the plan is 4,800 pairs, and the supplier needs six weeks to deliver a repeat order.


He committed 3,120 pairs before the season, 65% of the plan, and kept 1,680 pairs of budget open. A reorder placed in week 4 lands in week 10 and has six weeks to sell. One placed in week 8 lands in week 14, too late to sell at full price.


After four weeks, black was selling at 138% of the plan and tan at 61%. Tomas ordered 1,400 pairs of black in the four core sizes and released the remaining 280 pairs of budget to another category. Weather moves boot sales as well, so he read the first weeks against the temperature before trusting the trend.


## Depth per store: the last step of footwear inventory planning


Depth per store is where footwear inventory planning meets the stockroom. Two questions decide it: whether a store carries a model at all, and how many pairs it gets in each size.


### The presentation minimum sets a floor


A store that carries a model needs at least one pair in each size it offers. For a 12-size run, that is 12 pairs before any depth. A small store with a buy of 18 pairs has six pairs left to add to its core sizes.


After that, the five core sizes hold 11 of the 18 pairs, or 61% of the stock, for 65% of the demand. The split is close to right, but each core size has only two or three pairs. Below a certain buy, the better decision in footwear inventory planning is fewer models with a full run, or a shorter run in that store with the edge sizes available to order.


The buyers we work with often underestimate how many of their small stores sit under that threshold for a large part of the range.


### Measure broken runs as well as sell-through


A model can show a healthy sell-through while its core sizes are gone. The more useful measure for footwear inventory planning is the share of store and model combinations in which every core size is in stock. Reviewing it weekly shows where to send the next pairs.


Late in a season, the same measure supports consolidation. Priya, the chain's allocator, looked at a tan ankle boot in week 11 of 16 (an illustrative case). The chain had 192 pairs left, an average of eight per store across nine sizes, and only five of the 24 stores still had the four core sizes.


She pulled the remaining pairs out of the 14 slowest stores, 112 pairs in total, and sent them to the ten best. Those stores went from eight pairs to about 19 each, enough for a full run with two pairs in most sizes. The boot kept selling at full price in ten stores, where it would otherwise have sat broken in 24.


Our article on[rebalancing stock between stores](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/rebalancing-allocation-stores) covers how to check that a transfer pays for its own cost.


## A footwear inventory planning cycle in six steps


This footwear inventory planning cycle runs before each season for seasonal models and every month for carryover models.


1. **Split the range into carryover and seasonal models.** Give each group its own budget line, so that seasonal buys cannot use the money meant for weekly refills.
2. **Build size curves from clean history.** Use the weeks in which every size was in stock and at full price, net of returns. Build the curve by model family and by group of stores, since a city center store and a suburban store rarely share the same curve.
3. **Decide widths and edge sizes by store.** Carry the full run where the volume supports it. Elsewhere, shorten the run and serve the missing sizes from the warehouse.
4. **Set the opening depth and the reserve for seasonal models.** Fix the date after which a reorder can no longer arrive in time, and write it in the plan.
5. **Set size minimums for carryover models.** Calculate them by size and store from the sales rate and the delivery rhythm, then review them when the rate changes.
6. **Review broken runs every week.** Refill from the warehouse first, transfer between stores second, and consolidate the models that are ending.


Across Metreecs' work with footwear and fashion retailers, the weekly review in step 6 tends to be the first routine to slip when the team is busy. The damage from a skipped review only appears weeks later, as lost sales in the core sizes.


## Where footwear inventory planning still falls short


Three limits remain even when footwear inventory planning is done well, and each has a cause that can be named.


### Returns blur the demand by size


The NRF and Happy Returns estimated that 19.3% of online sales would be returned in 2025. Customers who order two sizes and send one back create sales in a size they never needed, so curves built on gross online sales lean toward the wrong sizes.


### New models have no curve of their own


A new last can fit half a size larger or smaller than the model it replaces. The borrowed curve is a starting point, and the first two or three weeks of sales and returns by size should correct it.


### Numbers per size and store are very small


In the carryover example, size 13 sells one pair every five to six weeks in a store. No method predicts in which week that pair will sell, so footwear inventory planning has to reason in probabilities and in cover.


That last limit is where a demand forecast by variant and by store helps most, because it pools the signal across sizes, stores, and similar models. Producing that forecast and turning it into replenishment proposals is what Metreecs does with AI-driven[inventory optimization](https://www.metreecs.com/inventory-optimization) . The decisions on range and brand stay with the buyer.


## FAQ


### How do you manage inventory in a shoe store?


Start from sales by size and width, corrected for the weeks when a size was missing. Hold a minimum per size for the models that run all year and refill them weekly. For seasonal models, buy an opening depth that follows the size curve and review broken runs every week.


### What is a size run in footwear?


A size run is the set of sizes in which a model is bought and stocked, for example US men's sizes 7 to 13 with half sizes. A full run puts every size on the shelf. A broken run is missing one or more sizes, usually the core sizes that sell fastest. Keeping runs complete is the main aim of footwear inventory planning in store.


### How many pairs per size should a shoe store stock?


There is no fixed number. Footwear inventory planning sets the quantity from the size curve of the store and the time between deliveries. In the example above, a store selling six pairs a week of a model holds three pairs of size 10 and one pair of size 13 with weekly refills.


### What is the difference between carryover and seasonal footwear?


Carryover models stay in the range for several seasons and are replenished continuously by size. Seasonal models are bought once for a selling window of a few months, with at most one reorder. They need separate budgets and separate rules in footwear inventory planning.


### How do you deal with broken size runs at the end of a season?


First refill from the warehouse if pairs remain. If they do not, consolidate: move the remaining pairs from the slowest stores to the best ones so that fewer stores hold a full run. Mark down only what is still incomplete after that.


## Conclusion


Footwear inventory planning comes down to the size run: curves built from clean history, separate rules for carryover and seasonal models, and a weekly look at which stores have lost their core sizes.
